title: He gives according to His treasury, not your expectations
subtitle: Al-Wahhab: the Bestower of gifts, freely, abundantly and beyond all hope
intro: Al-Wahhab (الْوَهَّابُ) means The Bestower: the One who gives gifts constantly, generously and freely, asking nothing in return, often in ways no one expected. Faith, children, a loving family, wisdom, even a kingdom: the Quran calls these His gifts. Knowing this name makes you ask Him boldly, even after you have made mistakes.

root.sense: Hibah is a gift: something given with nothing taken in exchange. Buying and selling are trades; a gift is the one transaction with no return. Gifts also tend to be unexpected and are not measured by what the receiver deserves. Al-Wahhab is the intensive form: the One who gives such gifts again and again, and gives great ones.

row.title: Ask small, I don't deserve much
sub: who am I to ask big

knowing: When someone gives you an envelope at a wedding, the amount usually reflects how generous and how wealthy they are, not what you deserve. {idea}Al-Wahhab gives according to His generosity and His limitless treasury{/idea}. The Arabic form is intensive: He is not one who gives a gift now and then, but the One who gives constantly, freely, and gifts of great value.

A gift differs from provision. Rizq is the sustenance Allah has guaranteed every creature. {idea}A hibah is beyond need and beyond deserving{/idea}: a surprise, unwrapped later, chosen out of the Giver's goodness rather than the receiver's merit. That is why the Quran uses this name for things no amount of effort can guarantee: a righteous child, a heart kept firm on faith.

His giving costs Him nothing. In a hadith qudsi in Sahih Muslim, Allah says that if every human and jinn, from first to last, stood in one place and asked, and He gave each what they asked, it would decrease what He has no more than a needle decreases the ocean when dipped into it.
seeing: Sulayman made a mistake, was tested, and turned back to Allah. Then, instead of a timid apology, he said: my Lord, forgive me, and grant me a kingdom such as no one after me will have; You are Al-Wahhab (38:35). {reward}He repented and asked big in the same breath{/reward}. He was given control over the wind and the jinn, something no amount of wealth can buy.

Most often, the Quran uses gift language for children. He gives daughters to whom He wills and sons to whom He wills (42:49). Zakariyya, old with a wife who had been barren, asked for an heir from Allah (19:5), and when the angels announced a son to Ibrahim's elderly wife, she called it an amazing thing (11:72); they answered: are you amazed at the decree of Allah? (11:73). The believers ask for spouses and children who are the comfort of their eyes (25:74), and the firmly grounded ask: our Lord, do not let our hearts swerve after You have guided us, and grant us mercy from Yourself; You are Al-Wahhab (3:8).
trusting: After a sin, we tend to shrink our duas. {trap}We ask for little because we feel we deserve little, as though His gifts were wages{/trap}. Sulayman's prayer corrects that. Repent sincerely, then ask Al-Wahhab for the great things: a righteous family, a pure heart, a high place in Paradise. The Prophet ﷺ told us to ask for al-Firdaws, the highest level, as recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari.

It helps with waiting too. Couples hoping for a child, parents praying for a child who has strayed, someone longing for a good spouse: these are all things the Quran calls gifts. You cannot earn them by effort alone, which is exactly why you ask the Bestower and keep asking, as Zakariyya and Ibrahim did for many years.
loving: We love people who surprise us with gifts we did not deserve. Look back at your life: faith you did not invent, people who love you, abilities you did not choose. {reward}All of it came from Al-Wahhab, unwrapped one day at a time{/reward}. Seeing it as gift rather than wage is where love starts.
now: It is the last ten nights of Ramadan. You are on the prayer mat, tired, about to whisper the same small dua as every year. Stop. Al-Wahhab gave Sulayman a kingdom right after his mistake. Ask Him tonight for the thing you have never dared to ask.
old: I keep my duas modest, because I do not think I deserve much from Allah.
new: Al-Wahhab gives by His generosity, not my merit, so I ask Him for great things.
try: Write down three big gifts you have never dared to ask Allah for, and ask Him for each one tonight, calling Him Ya Wahhab.

dua.text: Ya Wahhab, do not let my heart swerve after You have guided me. Grant me mercy from You, a family that is the comfort of my eyes, and gifts beyond what I know how to ask.
dua.note: This draws on the Quranic duas in 3:8 and 25:74; call on Him by this name especially when asking for faith, children and family.

pairs.why: Ar-Razzaq gives the provision every creature needs; Al-Wahhab gives gifts beyond need and beyond deserving.
Al-Fattah opens the closed door, and Al-Wahhab places the gift behind it.
His gifts flow from His generosity, so the Generous and the Bestower explain each other.

faq.a: Al-Wahhab means The Bestower or Giver of gifts. It is an intensive form describing the One who gives freely, constantly and abundantly, with nothing asked in return, and often in ways people never expected.

faq.q: How many times is Al-Wahhab mentioned in the Quran?
faq.a: Al-Wahhab appears three times: in 3:8, in the dua not to let our hearts swerve after guidance; in 38:9, about the treasures of His mercy; and in 38:35, in Sulayman's dua for a unique kingdom.

faq.q: What dua can I make with Ya Wahhab for children?
faq.a: Many people call on Allah as Al-Wahhab when asking for children, because the Quran describes children as His gift (42:49-50). You can also use Quranic prayers such as Zakariyya's request for good offspring (3:38) and the dua for families that are the comfort of the eyes (25:74).
